# Fasting vs. calorie restriction for weight loss: Which one wins?
## News briefs
If you're tired of counting calories to lose weight, you might consider a style of intermittent fasting called 4:3. It allows you to eat normally on four days of the week, and eat very little (fast) on the other three days, which can be spread throughout the week.
This approach might even help you lose more weight than counting calories, notes a small randomized controlled trial published in the May 20, 2025, issue of _Annals of Internal Medicine_ .

sources.snippet:
* A new study found that a 4:3 intermittent fasting plan—with three days of fasting per week—helped people lose more weight than daily calorie counting.
* The fasting group simply consumed fewer calories overall than the calorie-counting group, leading to greater weight loss.
* Talk to a healthcare provider before trying intermittent fasting, as it has several health risks and may be hard to stick to.

sources.title: Is Intermittent Fasting or Calorie Counting More Effective for Weight Loss?
sources.snippet: A study published in January 2023 in the _Journal of the American Heart Association_ found that after six years, participants who restricted calories lost more weight than those who continued an intermittent fasting diet.

answer: Intermittent fasting can produce more weight loss than daily calorie restriction, but results vary across studies. In a 2025 randomized trial of 165 people, those on a 4:3 fasting plan lost an average of about 6 more pounds after one year than the calorie-restriction group [2]. A meta-analysis of 17 publications (1,258 participants) found IF led to a more significant decrease in BMI than energy restriction, but the decrease in weight was slightly greater and statistically nonsignificant [1]. A 2024 meta-analysis found IF was more effective than continuous calorie restriction for weight loss, with no difference in BMI improvement [4]. A 2023 study found that after six years, participants who restricted calories lost more weight than those on intermittent fasting [6]. Another review concluded that IF (hypocaloric or eucaloric) and calorie restriction can be integrated into exercise training without negatively impacting most physical performance measures [5].
